clinicalPearls: A chronic hyperostotic and osteitic process centred on the sternum, medial clavicles and first ribs, causing anterior chest wall pain and bony swelling
Considered by many to be the anterior chest wall expression of SAPHO syndrome, and frequently accompanied by palmoplantar pustulosis
Presents with recurrent episodes of anterior chest pain and firm swelling over the sternoclavicular region, sometimes with restricted shoulder girdle movement
Bone scintigraphy classically demonstrates increased tracer uptake in the 'bull's head' distribution across the sternoclavicular joints
The process is sterile; cultures are negative and it is not a pyogenic infection despite the osteitis
Ossification and hyperostosis can compress adjacent structures, occasionally causing subclavian vein compression and venous congestion of the arm
Managed like SAPHO with NSAIDs first-line, and bisphosphonates or DMARDs including TNF inhibition for refractory disease
reference.pathophysiology: Sternocostoclavicular hyperostosis is a chronic sterile osteitis with reactive new bone formation affecting the sternum, medial clavicles and first ribs, and their connecting joints and ligaments. It is regarded as part of the SAPHO/autoinflammatory spectrum, in which dysregulated innate immunity drives neutrophilic bone inflammation and progressive hyperostosis and ossification of the anterior chest wall soft tissues and joints. The association with palmoplantar pustulosis and severe acne, and the proposed role of skin commensals such as Cutibacterium acnes as immune triggers, mirror the mechanisms of SAPHO syndrome. Progressive ossification produces bony expansion that can bridge joints and encroach on neurovascular structures at the thoracic inlet.
additionalDifferentials: Metastatic disease of the sternum or clavicle
Ankylosing spondylitis with anterior chest wall involvement
additionalInvestigations: Bone scintigraphy to demonstrate the anterior chest wall 'bull's head' uptake pattern
CT of the anterior chest wall to define hyperostosis, sclerosis and ossification
MRI to assess active osteitis and adjacent soft-tissue involvement
Inflammatory markers (ESR, CRP), often mildly to moderately raised
Venography or vascular imaging if subclavian vein compression is suspected
redFlags: Features of true infection (fever, rigors, positive cultures) requiring exclusion of septic arthritis or osteomyelitis
Destructive lesion or mass raising concern for malignancy
Arm swelling and venous distension suggesting subclavian vein compression or thrombosis
Rapidly progressive deformity or neurological symptoms at the thoracic inlet
reference.prognosis: The condition follows a chronic relapsing course; pain and swelling often persist over years, and although it is benign, progressive hyperostosis can cause lasting anterior chest wall discomfort and occasionally vascular compression.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing sterile osteitis as pyogenic infection and giving prolonged antibiotics or surgery
Failing to recognise the link with SAPHO syndrome and palmoplantar pustulosis
Overlooking subclavian vein compression as a cause of arm swelling
Attributing anterior chest pain to a cardiac cause and missing the bone pathology
